68515.etyen:
Ultimately of uncertain origin. Norwegian dialectal vingla (“to tumble about, wander to and fro”) is recorded by Ivar Aasen, first attested in 1850. Probably related to svinge (“to swing, sway”). Scandinavian etymological sources alternatively connect the word family with an older root denoting bending or curving, also represented in words related to vanke (“to wander”) and vinkel (“angle”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk vingle and vingla, dialectal Danish vingle and hvingle, Swedish vingla, Icelandic vingla and Faroese vingla (“to wobble, stagger”).

1000099.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Italian San Marino (“San Marino”), literally “Saint Marinus”, from san (“saint”), a short form of santo (“saint”), + the personal name Marino (“Marinus”). The country is named after Saint Marinus, who according to tradition founded a Christian community on Monte Titano in the fourth century.
The first element is ultimately from Latin sanctus (“holy; saint”). The personal name Marino continues Latin Marīnus (“Marinus”), a nominalisation of marīnus (“of the sea, marine”), from mare (“sea”).
Parallel international forms include Norwegian Nynorsk San Marino, Danish San M

1000611.etyen:
A 1995 respelling of Tchad, the former standard Norwegian spelling. The older form is ultimately from French Tchad, the French name of the country, which takes its name from Lake Chad.
The lake name is traditionally connected with Kanuri tsade (“lake; large expanse of water”). However, Gustav Nachtigal recorded the Kanuri name of the lake as Tsâd and reported that the name appeared to mean “large body of water” in the dialect of the earlier inhabitants of the western shore, the Sô and related peoples. The deeper linguistic origin is therefore uncertain. Modern Kanuri has Sádǝ for “Chad”.

1004707.etyen:
From stav (“staff, rod”) + sjø (“lake, sea”), with linking -s- (“interfix”) and the definite suffix -en (“definite singular suffix”), literally “the staff lake”. The first element stav (“staff, rod”) is from Old Norse stafr (“staff, stave”), from Proto-Germanic *stabaz (“staff, stick”). The second element sjø (“lake, sea”) is from Old Norse sjór (“sea”), from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz (“sea, lake”).
Compare Swedish Stavsjön (“place name”).

1004963.etyen:
Named after schoolteacher Daniel Trebonius, who taught at Stavanger Cathedral School from 1671. A Stavanger record from 1674 identifies him as Daniel Torbensen (Trebonius), while the University of Copenhagen matriculation already records him as Daniel Trebonius in 1652, showing that he used the learned name before coming to Norway.
